Research Report
A rare saccade velocity profile in Stiff-Person Syndrome with
cerebellar degeneration
Ari Z. Zivotofsky a,d, ⁎, Tali Siman-Tov b, Natan Gadoth b,c , Carlos R. Gordon b,c,d
aGonda Brain Research Center, Bar Ilan University, Ramat Gan 52900, Israel
bDepartment of Neurology, Meir General Hospital, Kfar-Saba 44281, Israel
cSackler Faculty of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University, Tel Aviv 69978, Israel
dEye Movement Laboratory, Rabin Medical Center, Petach Tiqva 49100, Israel
ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT
Article history:
Accepted 21 March 2006
Available online 24 May 2006
Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS) is an immune-mediated disorder of the central nervous system
characterized by muscle rigidity, episodic muscle spasms, and high titers of antibodies
against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). The presence of cerebellar ataxia in SPS is
extremely rare, but occurs. Clinical observations of ocular motor abnormalities have been
noted in a few SPS patients. The purpose of this study is to provide a detailed quantitative
documentation of ocular motor abnormalities in a patient with SPS and progressive
cerebellar signs. Detailed clinical assessment of a woman with SPS and precise eye
movement recordings using the magnetic search coil technique was performed. In addition
to other ocular motor abnormalities that included longer latencies for saccades, downbeat
nystagmus, and loss of downward smooth pursuit, a rare saccade velocity profile consisting
of multi-component saccades was observed. We postulate that these ocular motor findings
are related to impairment of GABAergic neurotransmission because antibodies to glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD-Abs) have been implicated in the pathogenesis of both SPS and
some cases of cerebellar ataxia. In addition, this unusual saccadic velocity profile may have
important implications for modeling the saccadic system and furthering a complete
understanding of saccade generation.

Ocular motor
GAD
Nystagmus
1. Introduction
Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS), previously also known as Stiff-
Man Syndrome, is an immune-mediated chronic disabling
disorder of the central nervous system characterized by
muscle rigidity, episodic muscle spasms, and high titers of
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) ( Levy et
al., 1999; Dalakas et al., 2000 ). GAD has been found to be a
major autoantigen in other disorders, especially in insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM). Recently, high levels of
GAD-Abs have also been reported in some patients with
cerebellar ataxia ( Honnorat et al., 1995; Saiz et al., 1997;
Honnorat et al., 2001 ).
The presence of cerebellar ataxia in SPS is extremely rare
and has been documented in only five case reports ( Giometto
et al., 1996; Brashear et al., 1997; Moldovanu et al., 1986; Kono
et al., 2001 ). Clinical observation of nystagmus has been
mentioned in only three of those five SPS patients (Giometto et
al., 1996; Moldovanu et al., 1986; Kono et al., 2001 ) and in some
patients with cerebellar ataxia and GAD-Abs ( Honnorat et al.,

1995; Honnorat et al., 2001 ). In a recent review of 68 SPS
patients, 14 had not defined “ocular motor disturbance ” and
five had “nystagmus and ataxia ” (Meinck and Thompson,
2002). A recent report (Economides and Horton, 2005) describes
the features of the nystagmus and the presence of additional
eye movement abnormalities in one patient using an infrared
system. We now present detailed documentation of ocular
motor abnormalities in a woman with SPS and progressive
cerebellar signs recorded using the scleral search coil. Because
it is speculated that the pathomechanism of spinal and
cerebellar signs in SPS is related to impairment of GABAergic
inhibitory neurotransmission due to GAD-Abs activity, we
conjecture that a similar mechanism may account for the
unusual eye movement abnormalities documented in our
patient.
2. Results
Horizontal smooth pursuit was preserved with a gain of 0.6 –
0.8. It was accompanied by approximately 2 or 3 corrective
saccades per second. Vertical smooth pursuit was direction-
ally dependent. In an upward pursuit, the patient had a gain of
0.6–0.7 with 3 –4 saccades per second. Downward pursuit was
essentially non-existent; at times, it reached a maximal gain
of 0.2 –0.3, while the majority of the time the tracking was
accomplished by means of a series of saccades.
The VOR in response to both sinusoidal chair rotation and
head thrust was normal. Furthermore, the caloric responses of
both ears were normal.
The latencies of horizontal and vertical saccades were
significantly longer (280 ± 57 ms and 349 ± 101 ms respectively)
as compared to normal control values of about 200 ms. The
latency for vertical saccades was significantly longer than that
for horizontal ( P < 0.001; two-sided t test with unequal
variance).
Vertical saccades showed an abnormal, rare velocity
profile. In the downward direction, multiple hypo-metric
saccades were used in order to reach the target. These
saccades were of normal velocity, albeit of smaller amplitude
than required, hence the need for multiple saccades. In these
multiple saccades, the eye stopped between saccades, and
only after a latency during which the eye was stationary did it
commence another saccade ( Fig. 1). In contrast, in the upward
direction, the target was reached not via multiple saccades,
but rather by means of a rare, multi-component single
saccade. The rare velocity profile of these saccades did not
reach zero between “sections” but rather contained several
peaks and valleys ( Fig. 2).
Similar to downward saccades, horizontal saccades, right-
ward and leftward, were usually accomplished by multiple
saccades (Fig. 3). The rare velocity profile of multi-component
saccades that do not reach zero between different segments of
the saccade was recorded in some occasions, although only in
rightward saccades ( Fig. 4).
On attempting fixation, there was an evident downbeating
nystagmus of small amplitude (0.5 –1.5° at 1.0 Hz) that was
interrupted by horizontal square wave jerks of about 0.5°
amplitude ( Fig. 5 ). The vertical nystagmus increased in
amplitude (to 2 –4°) and frequency (about 1.5 Hz) on left gaze
and was suppressed on right gaze. In Fig. 5, it is seen that the
slow phase of the downbeat nystagmus at times exhibits an
Fig. 1 – Sample of multiple saccade downward gaze shift. For
vertical eye movements, a positive movement is upward and
a negative is downward. The time axis is aligned with the
target step. The velocity is divided by 10 in order that it fit in

the same scale. Note that the gaze shift is accomplished by
means of two saccades each of which has normal metrics and
which are separated by a period of zero velocity.
Fig. 2 – Sample of multiple component upward saccades.
The time axis is aligned with the target step. Note that the
gaze shift is accomplished not by means of multiple saccades
each of which has normal metrics, but rather by one drawn
out saccade with multiple peaks. Unlike all the other graphs,
note that here the velocity is divided by 5.

exponential with increasing velocity and in other beats has a
decreasing exponential velocity. There was also a gaze-evoked
horizontal nystagmus of very small amplitude (about 0.5°).
A clear downbeating nystagmus with a slow phase velocity
of about 20–40°/s was recorded in the supine position by direct
current EOG. The amplitude was maximal a few seconds after
lying down. Following about 10 s, the amplitude decreased and
remained stable at about 15°/s. As in seated position, in supine
position, the nystagmus increased in amplitude on left gaze
and decreased in amplitude on right gaze.
3. Discussion
We provide a quantitative documentation of rare abnormal
saccades, downbeat nystagmus and loss of downward smooth
pursuit in a patient fulfilling the diagnostic requirements for
SPS (Levy et al., 1999; Dalakas et al., 2000 ) who later developed
progressive cerebellar ataxia.
The specific mechanism responsible for the clinical and
electrophysiological manifestations of SPS has not been yet
defined, but the accepted hypothesis assumes that impair-
ment of GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission, due to GAD-
Abs activity, causes continuous involuntary firing of motor
units, producing muscle stiffness ( Levy et al., 1999 ). Cerebellar
signs as a part of the clinical syndrome of SPS have previously
been reported in a few patients (Giometto et al., 1996; Brashear
et al., 1997; Moldovanu et al., 1986; Kono et al., 2001; Meinck
and Thompson, 2002). It is interesting to mention that a recent
study reviewing the clinical spectrum of anti-GAD-positive
SPS patients reports no cerebellar dysfunction in a series of 20
patients ( Dalakas et al., 2000 ). However, recent publications
describe an association between high titer of GAD-Abs and
subacute cerebellar ataxia ( Saiz et al., 1997; Honnorat et al.,
2001). The role of GAD-Abs in cerebellar dysfunction remains
to be elucidated, but it seems that the resulting presynaptic
impairment of inhibitory cerebellar synapses is responsible
for the cerebellar ataxia in these cases ( Ishida et al., 1999;
Mitoma et al., 2000). Nonetheless, the present case gives us the
possibility to examine the effects of impairment of GABAergic
inhibitory neurotransmission on ocular motor function.
Fig. 3 – Sample of multiple saccade horizontal gaze shifts. For
horizontal eye movements, a positive movement is
rightward and a negative is leftward. Note that both
rightward and leftward gaze shifts are accomplished by
means of multiple saccades, each of which has normal
metrics and which are separated by a period of zero velocity.
Fig. 4 – Sample of multiple component rightward saccade.
Note that this rightward gaze shift is accomplished by means
of one drawn out saccade with multiple peaks and that at no
time does the gaze velocity reach zero before the conclusion
of the entire movement.
Fig. 5 – Horizontal and vertical eye movements during
attempted fixation. Note that in the vertical plane there is a
downbeating nystagmus of small amplitude and in the
horizontal plane there are square wave jerks.

On first examination after at least 3 years of complaints
of stiffness, the neurological examination of our patient
disclosed slow saccades and mild right-sided cerebellar
signs. On subsequent examination 6 months later, she
complained of positional ve rtigo, and on neurological
examination, a clear downbeating nystagmus was found
when lying down. At this time, quantitative, precise eye
movement recordings revealed saccade abnormalities that
included prolonged latencies and a rare velocity profile
particularly in the upward direction, downbeat nystagmus,
and loss of downward smooth pursuit.
The velocity curve of normal saccades is continuous and
smooth, reaching a peak and then monotonically descending
back to zero. There are a few reports of atypical velocity
profiles ( Abel et al., 1987; Rottach et al., 1996 ). The difference
between those previously reported atypical saccades and the
ones documented here is that those saccades do not show a
reversal of direction in the velocity profile and the saccades
shown here (Figs. 2 and 4) do exhibit such a reversal. Although
the direction of the eye movement does not change, there is a
change in the direction of the acceleration. The saccade was
ending, i.e. decelerating, but instead of continuing to do so, it
again accelerated as if a new saccade was being superimposed
on the terminating saccade. This phenomenon of multi-
component saccades may be similar to what Jack et al. (1997)
reported and was quantitatively first reported in the literature
in a study of eye movements in late-onset Tay –Sachs disease
(LOTS) (Rucker et al., 2004 ). These authors postulated that the
abnormalities seen in the velocity profile may be explained by
a disruption of a “latch circuit” that normally inhibits pontine
omnipause neurons, permitting burst neurons to discharge
until the eye movement is completed.
Alternatively, two other explanations related to the burst
neurons and the omnipause neurons that govern the gener-
ation of saccades can be offered for the phenomenon observed
in our patient ( Leigh and Zee, 1999 ). Instead of the burst
neurons firing in a synchronized manner and generating a
saccade with a unified peak, due to impaired GABAergic
transmission, they fire in a non-synchronized manner that
results in the multiple-peaked saccades seen. Alternatively,
the flaw can be due to some of the omnipause neurons
inappropriately commencing firing before the saccade is
completed and then again silencing, either due to a problem
in the latch mechanism or because of an inherent problem in
the omnipause neurons. Interestingly, Robinson (2000) has
shown that when injecting the GABAa agonist muscimol
among saccade-related neurons in the cerebellar posterior
interpositus nucleus the velocities of upward and downward
saccades were differentially affected, as were the upward and
downward saccades in this patient.
The inherent problem with the omnipause neurons can
be an elevated threshold required to turn them off. Thus,
they start firing too early. This would also explain the
increased saccadic latency. In order to generate a saccade,
the omnipause neurons must be silenced. With an elevated
threshold, they remain active, resulting in an increased
saccadic latency. Several other explanations related to a
decrease of normal GABA inhibition at different CNS levels
can also be offered for the increased latencies. For example,
injection of GABA antagonist bicuculline into the rostral pole

of the superior colliculus increased saccadic latency ( Hiko-
saka and Wurtz, 1985 ).
Downbeat nystagmus is commonly associated with lesions
of the vestibulocerebellum and underlying medulla ( Leigh and
Zee, 1999). Experimental ablation of the flocculus in monkeys
removes inhibition from the anterior canal projections
producing downbeat nystagmus ( Zee et al., 1981 ). It is known
that loss of Purkinje cell function in the midline structures of
the posterior cerebellum could lead to a disinhibition of
anterior semicircular canal input, resulting in upward drift of
the eyes and consequently downbeat nystagmus. A GABAergic
pathway from Purkinje cells to the flocculus has been
described ( Babalian and Vidal, 2000 ), and GAD-Abs could
possibly affect this transmission causing downbeat nystag-
mus. The amplitude of the downbeat nystagmus of our patient
was clearly increased in the supine position. This effect of
gravity is a well-recognized phenomenon in many cases of
downbeat nystagmus that has been explained by an imbal-
ance of the otolith-ocular reflex pathway ( Rude and Baker,
1996; Marti et al., 2002 ). The waveform of the slow phase of
downbeat nystagmus seen in Fig. 5 appears to have an
exponential time course, with increasing or decreasing
velocity suggesting an unstable neural integrator ( Leigh and
Zee, 1999 ). Based on the fact that, in our patient, vertical
smooth pursuit was directionally dependent, her downbeat
nystagmus could also be explained by imbalance of vertical
smooth pursuit tone (Zee et al., 1974). The upward pursuit was
saccadic with a gain of 0.6 –0.7, while downward pursuit was
essentially non-existent. Recent evident ( Glausauer et al.,
2004) indicates that downward pursuit is impaired in down-
beat nystagmus, and this is compatible with the absence of
downward smooth pursuit in this patient.
Recent reports of patients with downbeat nystagmus and
periodic alternating nystagmus and GAD-Abs but without SPS
have been described (Antonini et al., 2003; Tilikete et al., 2005 ).
The only additional eye movement abnormality reported in
these patients was slow vertical saccades in one of the
patients with downbeat nystagmus.
The rare saccadic velocity profile seen in our patient that
had not been previously described until a little over a year ago
could have important implications in models of saccade
generation and in furthering an in-depth, comprehensive,
understanding of the saccadic system. Further studies using
precise measurement of eye movement are warranted to
provide a better understanding of ocular motor abnormalities
in patients with GAD-Abs. In addition, finding additional
patients with multi-component saccades would further assist
in unraveling the cause of this unusual phenomenon that we
observed in our patient and that probably exists in persons
with other diseases. Understanding the cause of this atypical
velocity profile can possibl y shed light on the normal
functioning of the saccadic system.
4. Experimental procedures
4.1. Clinical assessment
All protocols were approved by the ethics committee of
Beilinson Hospital, adhered to the tenets of the Declaration
138 BRAIN RESEARCH 1093 (2006) 135 – 140

of Helsinki, and written informed consent was obtained from
the patient for all parts of the study.
A 46-year-old woman complained of lower back pain,
progressive tightness, and painful spasm of muscles of both
legs and abdomen for the last 3 years. On examination, she
had profound lumbar lordosis, extreme painful stiffness of
the abdominal wall, increased muscle tone in the left leg,
brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Trömner and Hoffmann
signs, and flexor plantar responses. Cerebellar function
examination disclosed mild right-sided limb dysmetria and
dysdiadochokinesis. The gait was slow, wide-based, and
unsteady. Needle electromyography revealed continuous
motor unit activity of rectus abdominis and paraspinal
muscles at rest, which was completely abolished after
10 mg of intravenous diazepam. A shortened silent period
was recorded from all four extremities after transcranial
magnetic stimulation. A meticulous laboratory work-up
disclosed pernicious anemia, family history of IDDM, and
the presence of HLA alleles DQB1 0201 and DRB1 0301.
Serum titer of GAD-Abs was markedly increased (81,858 U/
ml; normal <1000). The various forms of hereditary cerebel-
lar ataxia were ruled out by the appropriate molecular
genetic tests. Anti-Yo and anti-Hu antibodies were negative
and brain MRI was normal. During 1 year of follow-up and
prior to the present recording of ocular movements, there
was a modest benefit from intravenous immunoglobulins
and a much more significant benefit from daily oral
diazepam. However, a progressive impairment of eye move-
ments was documented. Initially, the range of voluntary eye
movements was full in all directions, but horizontal and
vertical saccades were slow. It also seemed that smooth
pursuit and vestibulo-ocular reflexes were normal. On a
follow-up visit 6 months later, she complained of positional
vertigo, and on examination, downbeating nystagmus was
present when she was lying down; this was most prominent
on left gaze.
4.2. Eye movement recordings and data analysis
The experimental paradigms and data collection were done
using Labview (National Instrument), and analysis of the
data was performed using Matlab. Horizontal and vertical
gaze of the right eye and head rotations were measured
using the magnetic search coil technique ( Robinson, 1963 )
with 6-ft field coils (CNC Engineering, Seattle, WA) using a
scleral search coil embedded in a silastic ring (Skalar, Delft,
Netherlands). The eye movement recordings were monocu-
lar because clinically all eye movements appeared to be
conjugate, and there was no clinical complaint of diplopia.
The coils were pre-calibrated using a protractor device. The
coil was placed on the eye after application of two drops of
local anesthetic (benoxinate HCl 0.4%). Coil signals were
filtered (bandwidth 0 –200 Hz) prior to digitization at 500 Hz
sampling rate, with 12-bit resolution. The visual stimulus
was a red laser spot (1.5 mm diameter) rear-projected onto
a semitranslucent screen situated 1.1 m in front of the
subject. The position of the laser spot was determined by
an X –Y galvanometer. The subject sat in front of the screen
in a dark room and was given time to adjust to the dark.
Her head was immobilized with a head restraint device
attached to the chair. Smooth pursuit eye movements were
tested by having the subject track a target moving at 10°/s
from eccentric (between 7.5 and 15°) positions to the origin.
Saccades were tested by having the target step right, left,

up, or down along one of the principal axes between 5 and
15°. VOR was measured by rotating the chair in a sinusoidal
manner back and forth at approximately 0.4 Hz. In addition,
the response to head thrusts was measured by asking the
patient to fixate her gaze on the laser spot target, while her
head was held from behind by one of the investigators who
executed sudden, rapid, unpredictable angular head rota-
tions to both sides.
Direct current electro-oculgraphic (EOG) recording was
performed to measure positional downbeating nystagmus
and vestibular response to standard caloric stimulation. The
EOG was utilized for these two tests because the coil system is
not set up for use with a supine subject.

4.2. Eye movement recordings and data analysis
The experimental paradigms and data collection were done
using Labview (National Instrument), and analysis of the
data was performed using Matlab. Horizontal and vertical
gaze of the right eye and head rotations were measured
using the magnetic search coil technique ( Robinson, 1963 )
with 6-ft field coils (CNC Engineering, Seattle, WA) using a
scleral search coil embedded in a silastic ring (Skalar, Delft,
Netherlands). The eye movement recordings were monocu-
lar because clinically all eye movements appeared to be
conjugate, and there was no clinical complaint of diplopia.
The coils were pre-calibrated using a protractor device. The
coil was placed on the eye after application of two drops of
local anesthetic (benoxinate HCl 0.4%). Coil signals were
filtered (bandwidth 0 –200 Hz) prior to digitization at 500 Hz
sampling rate, with 12-bit resolution. The visual stimulus
was a red laser spot (1.5 mm diameter) rear-projected onto
a semitranslucent screen situated 1.1 m in front of the
subject. The position of the laser spot was determined by
an X –Y galvanometer. The subject sat in front of the screen
in a dark room and was given time to adjust to the dark.
Her head was immobilized with a head restraint device
attached to the chair. Smooth pursuit eye movements were
tested by having the subject track a target moving at 10°/s
from eccentric (between 7.5 and 15°) positions to the origin.
Saccades were tested by having the target step right, left,

15°. VOR was measured by rotating the chair in a sinusoidal
manner back and forth at approximately 0.4 Hz. In addition,
the response to head thrusts was measured by asking the
patient to fixate her gaze on the laser spot target, while her
head was held from behind by one of the investigators who
executed sudden, rapid, unpredictable angular head rota-
tions to both sides.
Direct current electro-oculgraphic (EOG) recording was
performed to measure positional downbeating nystagmus
and vestibular response to standard caloric stimulation. The
EOG was utilized for these two tests because the coil system is
not set up for use with a supine subject.
